articles.title: Sino-US forum held in HK ahead of Apec summit
articles.excerpt: Global leaders across various fields will gather in Hong Kong ahead of the Apec leaders' summit in Shenzhen to discuss…
articles.fullText:
Global leaders across various fields will gather in Hong Kong ahead of the Apec leaders' summit in Shenzhen to discuss how Sino-US relations can be reshaped in search of long-term stability and cooperation.

The annual US-China Hong Kong Forum will be held between November 15 and 17.

James Chau, president of the organisers China-United States Exchange Foundation, said dozens of speakers would be joining the event, including former vice foreign minister Cui Tiankai, members of the Nixon and Bush families from the US, and former Thailand prime minister Abhisit Vejjajiva.

“Through this forum we also bring regional perspectives into the discussion," Chau said.

"So we've got Asean, for example, represented by Thailand, but also by Singapore. The [Sino-US] relationship affects more than two countries, so there's always that temptation to look at our work simply through the bilateral lens of China and the United States.

“I wish it was like that because it seems very tidy, neat and easy to follow. But, in fact, everything that these two countries do and don't do, what they think and what they consider, is going to impact over eight billion people all around the world.”

More than 300 participants will take part in the open forum on the second day, among them a group of university students from around the world.

“Having young people in the room who are 18 to 25 years old who come from phenomenal schools of public policy and who would have spent part of the private sessions with us and then into the public sessions, we want them to ask the very first question during the audience Q&A to keep those leaders on the stage very sharp,” Chau said.

The Apec summit will be held on November 18-19 in Shenzhen.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: 'A Symphony of Lights' to go out with a bang next week
articles.excerpt: The Tourism Board said a multimedia light show that has been a nightly fixture across Victoria Harbour for more than…
articles.fullText:
The Tourism Board said a multimedia light show that has been a nightly fixture across Victoria Harbour for more than two decades will be performed one last time on November 18.

Board chairman Peter Lam said on Tuesday it's time to bring the curtain down on "A Symphony of Lights", which has thrilled millions of locals and visitors alike since 2004.

"A Symphony of Lights, which has accompanied us in Hong Kong for 22 years, will perform its final show... with added pyrotechnic elements to commemorate this meaningful moment," he said.

"As for other light and projection shows, we will continue to roll them out gradually next year."

Financial Secretary Paul Chan, who announced a string of initiatives in this year's budget to enhance the city's tourism appeal, has said the long-running show will be replaced by "light festivals across various locations at different times of the year".

Meanwhile, Lam said revellers can look forward to Hong Kong WinterFest, which will run from November 18 to January 5.

He said that the annual Christmas and New Year celebrations will be the biggest ever.

Under "Winter Wonderland", three festive installations will go up in Central, Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay, including a 22-metre Christmas tree at Statue Square Gardens.

The traditional New Year's Eve countdown will culminate in a fireworks display over Victoria Harbour.

There will also be shopping and dining discounts.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Tech gains, oil price falls lift HK, mainland markets
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong and mainland stocks closed higher on Tuesday, led by AI supply chain shares, as an overnight rally on…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong and mainland stocks closed higher on Tuesday, led by AI supply chain shares, as an overnight rally on Wall Street and sliding oil prices lifted risk sentiment across Asia.

The benchmark Hang Seng Index closed 108 points, or 0.4 percent, higher at 24,557 on turnover of HK$178.17 billion.

The tech index rose 43 points, or 1.1 percent, to 4,084 while the China enterprises index crept five points, or 0.1 percent, up to 8,265.

Optical communication giant Zhongji Innolight jumped nine percent while Wuxi AppTec rose up to five percent before paring gains after the Pentagon removed the biotechnology company from its list of Chinese military companies.

Mainland chip firms Suzhou Denglin Technology and Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology made mixed trading debuts after raising a combined HK$2.36 billion in initial public offerings.

AI chip designer Suzhou Denglin ended HK$18, or 7.79 percent, down at HK$213 while semiconductor packager and tester Jiangsu Xinde was HK$2.52, or 28 percent, up at HK$11.40.

On the mainland, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index inched up just under three points, or 0.08 percent, to end at 3,663.

The Shenzhen Component Index was 96 points, or 0.86 percent, higher at 11,241 while the ChiNext Index was 35 points, or 1.46 percent, up at 2,494.

Chip supply chain shares across Asia climbed, tracking an overnight rally on Wall Street that saw the Nasdaq jump 2.7 percent.

The 5G Communication Index rose 2.6 percent, leading gains onshore, while the tech-focused Star50 Index was up nearly one percent.

Non-ferrous metal shares edged up 0.1 percent as gold prices rebounded this month on falling oil prices.

The CSI Energy Index fell 2.6 percent, with PetroChina down 6.3 percent.

China's trade surplus surged past US$1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei climbed up by 1,684 points, or 2.87 percent, to end at 60,459, extending its rebound from a tech-led selloff on Friday as AI-related stocks surged.

The broader Topix was up 75 points, or 1.98 percent, at 3,893.

In Seoul, the Kospi closed up 220 points, or 4.39 percent, at 5,239 in a sharp rebound from nine-month lows as chipmakers tracked overnight gains in US tech stocks. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK five-year plan offers UK long-term prospects: CE
articles.excerpt: Chief Executive John Lee on Tuesday said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan offered long-term prospects for UK companies, investors, and…
articles.fullText:
Chief Executive John Lee on Tuesday said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan offered long-term prospects for UK companies, investors, and institutions and reinforced the city’s role as a bridge between China and the world.

In a speech delivered at the British Chamber of Commerce, Lee pointed to the scale of the existing UK-Hong Kong economic relationship, noting that 770 British companies had a presence in the city last year, up seven percent year on year.

Merchandise trade between the two places reached nearly US$20 billion last year, up 26 percent over 2024, while the UK ranked fourth in inward direct investment into Hong Kong and sixth in outward direct investment from the city at the end of 2024.

"Those numbers reflect the strong ties between us. They also underline the continuing confidence British companies and investors have in Hong Kong," he said.

Lee said the city's inaugural blueprint reinforced Hong Kong’s "four centres and one hub" – its status as an international financial, shipping and trade centre, its development into an international innovation and technology centre and its role as a hub for high-calibre talent.

He also identified the Northern Metropolis as a key growth engine under the plan and as a way to deepen Hong Kong’s participation in the Greater Bay Area – a cluster of some 88 million people with a combined GDP comparable to the world’s tenth-largest economy.

The project, adjacent to Shenzhen, will include three university towns spanning more than 1,000 hectares, with 300 hectares dedicated to campuses and the remainder to technology, industry, residential and recreational development.

Lee invited UK companies, investors, universities and research institutions to explore opportunities there in life and health technology, AI, robotics and microelectronics.

He also noted that Hong Kong’s five universities rank among the world’s top 100, and said the time was ripe to expand post-secondary collaboration with the UK.

He pointed to a recent London talent showcase – part of three UK events that together drew more than 4,500 visits – as reflecting British interest in career opportunities in Hong Kong.

Lee stressed the complementary nature of the UK-Hong Kong relationship, citing shared financial standards and different time zones.

"With our similar financial standards, and different time zones – one of us is on the day shift, while the other is on the night shift, covering the whole clock together," he said.

"Complementarity has long been one of the reasons you have confidence in the flourishing future we're building together."

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Minibus driver arrested for alleged drug driving
articles.excerpt: A 44-year-old minibus driver was arrested on suspicion of drug driving on Tuesday after a rapid oral fluid test indicated…
articles.fullText:
A 44-year-old minibus driver was arrested on suspicion of drug driving on Tuesday after a rapid oral fluid test indicated he had taken methamphetamine before operating the vehicle.

Acting on intelligence, officers from the Kowloon East traffic headquarters' enforcement and control division mounted a targeted operation, focusing on a driver operating a green minibus route between Yau Tong and the Anderson public transport terminus.

Police intercepted the minibus and escorted seven passengers off the vehicle before conducting an oral fluid screening test on the driver.

Preliminary investigations found he had consumed meth before driving, resulting in his immediate arrest.

"This type of behaviour is not merely a violation, but poses a serious threat to the lives of passengers and other road users," senior inspector Poon Chun-ho said.

He said drivers who knowingly take drugs that impair judgement and reaction but still operate public transport are placing the safety of every passenger at extreme risk, with potentially catastrophic consequences.

The driver has been denied bail and is due to appear at Kwun Tong Magistrates' Courts on Wednesday.

The operation followed the arrest of three other minibus and taxi drivers on suspicion of drug driving in June.

Poon said two of them have since been convicted, with one slapped with a two-month jail term and a driving ban of two years and the other sentenced to four months in prison and receiving a five-year driving ban.

The third driver has been released on bail pending trial.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: 'SZ, HK should join hands to grow external trade'
articles.excerpt: As Shenzhen's maritime logistics industry has taken off in recent years, a senior official at one of the world's busiest…
articles.fullText:
As Shenzhen's maritime logistics industry has taken off in recent years, a senior official at one of the world's busiest container terminals said Hong Kong still had much to offer as the nation forges closer ties with the world.

Yantian Port, in eastern Shenzhen, is a vital gateway between the nation's manufacturing engine and global markets.

It handles more than one-third of Guangdong's foreign trade and a quarter of the country's container exports to the United States.

According to the Shenzhen municipal government, the deep-water port handled 16.1 million TEUs, or twenty-foot equivalent units, in 2025, representing a 7.1 percent year-on-year increase.

Lawrence Shum, managing director of Yantian, a subsidiary of Hutchison Ports, said the terminal operates nearly 100 international routes on a weekly basis.

Fifty-three of those routes are linked to Apec economies.

"Since the start of this year, we have added 14 new routes to and from Apec economies, further expanding our international network and fostering regional trade," he said.

"According to the customs figures, Shenzhen continues to lead the country in both imports and exports to Apec economies. We even set a record in the first nine months of this year, with a trade value of 3.23 trillion yuan, a 40 percent jump."

Shenzhen is the host of this year's Apec leaders' summit scheduled for November 18 and 19.

Shum explained that Yantian had a unique advantage over other Shenzhen ports when handling shipments from inland regions.

"Yantian houses Shenzhen's only railway that reaches directly into the port area. Through sea‑rail intermodal transport, port services can be extended to inland regions such as the southwest and central areas, making it more convenient for enterprises in Chengdu and Chongqing and bringing them closer to international markets," he said.

Under Shenzhen's 15th Five-Year Plan, Yantian is to strengthen cooperation with Hong Kong's Kwai Tsing Container Terminals.

Shum said six daily vessel trips between the two ports mean cargo can arrive at its destination in about six to eight hours.

"For inland foreign trade enterprises, transportation time can be more stable, more efficient, and more environmentally friendly. Shenzhen and Hong Kong can further tap into inland cargo trade ... and achieve a win‑win for the three regions," Shum said.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: US 'pulls warplanes from new UK base over Iran threat'
articles.excerpt: The US military has evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in Britain after a threat from Iran, the Wall Street…
articles.fullText:
The US military has evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in Britain after a threat from Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, weeks after a suspected Iran-linked security incident at the RAF Fairford airbase led to the withdrawal of US bombers.

Two US refuelling tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base diverted to Germany earlier on Monday morning while several other tankers at the base were moved to Germany and other locations later in the day, the report said.

According to the Journal, the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among US officials.

“We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” a British ministry of defence spokesperson said.

Five British men were arrested outside the RAF Fairford base in southwest England in September, prompting the US to remove its B-1 bombers from that airbase shortly after on security grounds.

RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Covid booster uptake stalls among high-risk groups
articles.excerpt: The Hong Kong Doctors Union warned that the city’s Covid-19 booster programme is losing momentum, citing low uptake among older…
articles.fullText:
The Hong Kong Doctors Union warned that the city’s Covid-19 booster programme is losing momentum, citing low uptake among older adults and high-risk groups and limited access to vaccines in the community.

According to the latest statistics from the Centre for Health Protection, only 717 Covid-19 booster doses were administered last month.

Over the past 12 months, a total of 47,828 Covid-19 vaccines were administered in Hong Kong, said Ivan Hung, chair of infectious diseases and vaccinology in the department of medicine at the University of Hong Kong.

Of these, 46,119 went to people aged 50 or above.

Based on a population of about 3.62 million in that age range, the doses equate to only about 1.27 percent – reflecting a low vaccination rate among older adults.

A questionnaire by the union found that 79 percent of the 300 doctors surveyed considered vaccination among older adults unsatisfactory.

Nearly 40 percent said they did not proactively remind patients about Covid-19 jabs, while almost 60 percent of these doctors cited not having vaccines on hand.

Hung warned that Hong Kong has annual Covid-19 seasonality and that the disease should not be taken lightly.

"We expect the next surge to happen in probably a year's time, and when the antibodies drop to a low level, then there will be another surge of Covid," he said.

Hung pointed to data from the centre showing that there had been more than 170 severe cases or deaths in the recent period, describing the figure as large for high-risk individuals.

He said access is a key barrier.

Only 58 public vaccination points, the union noted, remain at present and just 18 private clinics are designated Covid-19 vaccination stations, compared with the more than 1,000 private clinics offering flu jabs under the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme.

Many people think Covid-19 is a relatively mild disease, Hung said, but high-risk groups do need boosters every six months.

The union called for routine Covid-19 vaccine supplies under the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme, one-stop flu and Covid-19 jabs at family doctor clinics, and stronger public education.

Hung stressed the importance of making the process simple, especially for older adults.

"The current vaccination programme could be similar to that of the flu vaccination; that means that if you want to get a Covid-19 booster, then you don't need to get registered online," he said.

"We just simply walk into a general practice and get vaccinated, similar to that of the flu shot, and the criteria for getting a Covid-19 shot should be similar to that of the flu shot, then that makes things easier for both the doctors and the older adults."

Medical professionals urged priority groups to receive updated vaccines on time to maintain immune protection, with such groups including the elderly, those with chronic diseases, those who are expecting and healthcare workers.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Australia to be AI first-mover with safety regulator
articles.excerpt: Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website…
articles.fullText:
Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by a rogue OpenAI agent in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday.

The regulator would enforce world-leading legislated AI standards that would apply to all frontier AI companies that want to operate in Australia, he said.

Financial penalties would apply, although the government has yet to detail those penalties.

“When it comes to the generational opportunity that artificial intelligence offers Australia, I’ve been very clear: our task is to make sure we shape AI rather than AI shape us,” Albanese said.

“Australia is the first mover in this space and we want to make sure that we continue to work so that we can reap the potential benefits from AI.”

AI standards would mandate rapid incident notifications.

The standards would include companies maintaining security controls across all stages of models’ development and deployment, as well as identifying and managing serious risks.

The standards also would mandate rapid notification to the government of incidents such as “misaligned behaviour” conflicting with developers' intentions.

Australian government documents define frontier AI as the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability.

Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the US company took too long to inform the government in September that a rogue agent had infiltrated government websites three months earlier, which was the first occurrence of such a breach with the technology.

Information taken without authorisation from the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18 has since been made public.

It is not clear whether the portal breach broke any Australian laws.

OpenAI apologised in September for the breach and its slow response.

“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement.

“We also should have handled our response better.”

A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations including that the government consider changing the law.

Albanese said his government had accepted all the inquiry’s recommendations, including for potential criminal law reform.

“The point is law needs to get ahead of and in some cases make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world. And to be clear, Australia is a first-mover in these areas,” Albanese said.

The proposed AI regulator would follow Australia appointing an eSafety Commissioner in 2015.

The office describes itself as the world’s first government agency dedicated to keeping people safer online.

Since December, the commissioner has been enforcing a world-first ban on Australian children younger than 16 holding accounts on popular social media platforms. (AP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: No internet, no advance warning: 11 killed in Myanmar military bombing in Sagaing
articles.excerpt: Civilians in war zones are left vulnerable as Starlink internet becomes scarce after scam center crackdown.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
It was just before noon on Saturday. Three gyrocopters flew low as they approached Nyaung Pin Lay village. A school and surrounding residential area was bombed. Eleven were killed, including four children.
A resident told RFA that although the local People’s Defense Forces (PDF) received a tip that the Myanmar military would bomb the school, the warning could not reach them in time due to the lack of internet in the village.
“Information that this would be bombed was sent online to everyone. They did inform us,” the Kani Township resident told RFA on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“But because there was no Starlink communication, casualties were high as a result. About a month ago in Nat La Po village, when we got the exact location that would be bombed and cleared the area, there were no casualties. That was fortunate. But now, even though we got the location to be bombed, communication was cut off.”
A May 25, 2025, photo shows a Starlink sign at an internet cafe in Demoso, Myanmar.
(AFP) In Myanmar, home to the world’s longest-running civil war, the military-appointed government has cut off phone lines and internet communications in over 40 percent of townships nationwide. Locals, civil society groups, and revolutionary forces tell RFA that they rely on Starlink — acquiring the devices through unofficial and often expensive channels — as a lifeline for information.
In October 2025, SpaceX announced the disabling of over 2,500 Starlink kits in Myanmar to crack down on transnational cyber-scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border. Subsequent restrictions by SpaceX on unregistered units bought outside of Myanmar have shut down countless others.
Since June, more than 20 percent of Starlink internet devices used in Myanmar have had their services cut off, according to a report released on Oct. 23 by the group Athan.
Local residents and human rights activists told RFA that this has created a crisis for the survival of civilians in areas of intense civil conflict.
A Myanmar government photo taken on Oct. 20, 2025, shows seized Starlink devices during a raid on the KK Park online scam center in Myawaddy.
(Myanmar Military Information Team via AFP) “The military cutting off phone lines and internet connections from the start was intentionally aimed at concealing human rights violations they commit and restricting people’s freedom of expression,” said Joy, a research director at Athan, a non-profit organization for the Freedom of Expression Movement in Myanmar.
“If Starlink also stops providing services to Myanmar and cuts connections, emergency humanitarian aid, air strike alerts, news regarding military columns, and natural disaster warnings for these local residents will stop immediately.”
According to a report titled “Dead Air” released by Athan on October 23, the communication cut-off directly affects the lives and safety of people in conflict-affected regions as they can no longer receive warnings about airstrikes and military movements, medical aid, or updates on family members’ safety and evacuation routes.
RFA contacted Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military-appointed president’s office, regarding when internet and phone lines might be restored. She instead referred RFA to the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications.
Now, not only Starlink devices used by scam operations are being shut down, but Starlink connections used by civilians have also been suspended starting in June this year, with more than 20 percent of devices cut off by October, according to Athan. Consequently, regions like Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, Rakhine, Kayah State, and other areas experiencing severe conflict were directly affected, Athan’s report states.
RFA contacted SpaceX regarding the impact on civilians in regions where the internet has been cut off, but has not received a response at the time of publication.
“Some of our Starlink devices were disabled. This has caused a lot of trouble for us,” said Ma Aye Myint Aung Aung, Head of the Department of Humanitarian Assistance and Emergency Management under the Mandalay Regional Interim Administrative Council.
“On the other hand, whether it’s our civilians, revolutionary groups, or those leading and operating the administrative mechanism in revolutionary forces, everyone relies on Starlink. As access to information becomes more restricted, limitations on civilian safety also increase. I would define this as a very major challenge for us.”
In Kayah State, Deputy Minister of Defense for the Karenni State Government Khu Daniel told RFA that Starlink connections are being shut down one by one, raising concerns.
“For the public and for the youth currently fighting in battle, it will become a cause for concern,” he said.
A Sept. 17, 2025, photo shows people on a balcony of a building with what appears to be Starlink satellite dishes on the roof in the KK Park complex in Myawaddy, Myanmar.
(Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP) Khun Chit Htoo, who is assisting refugees in the Karenni Region, said that if all Starlink services are shut down, it could have a severe impact on humanitarian aid operations.
“Our current work relies on internet connectivity as well as donors. Since we connect online, we are very concerned,” said Khun Chit Htoo.
“We will face a situation where we can no longer help needy civilians receive the support they really need across all aspects of coordination. If there is no internet line left, I believe we stand to lose a lot because of this single connection.”
While welcoming and supporting the shutdown of Starlink internet lines used by online scam operations to crack down on scam syndicates, 317 civil society organizations issued a statement on July 17 expressing deep concern over potential negative impacts if all Starlink terminals nationwide are shut down.
According to an October 23 report by the Myanmar Internet Project, an organization monitoring internet shutdowns and conflicts, there were 581 military airstrikes that killed at least 353 civilians in the three months from July to September 2026, with 562 of those attacks occurring in areas where internet service was cut off.
Translated by Nayrein Kyaw. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: Balmy weather set to overtake cool spell later in week
articles.excerpt: The Observatory recorded a low of 17.5 degrees Celsius in urban areas on Tuesday morning – the lowest since autumn…
articles.fullText:
The Observatory recorded a low of 17.5 degrees Celsius in urban areas on Tuesday morning – the lowest since autumn began this year.

Acting senior scientific officer Lam Hok-yin said the city was being affected by relatively strong northerly winds.

"When it's windy, body heat is easily blown away, so it feels colder," he said.

"Everyone's constitution is different – so when it's windy and cold, we urge people to put on an extra layer before heading out."

Lam said Wednesday morning would still be relatively cool, with urban temperatures around 18 degrees and the New Territories at least one or two degrees lower.

But with sunny and dry weather, daytime temperatures may rise to around 25 degrees and should climb further later in the week, he pointed out.

Looking ahead to winter, he said under the influence of global warming and the super El Niño, Hong Kong's temperatures are very likely to be normal to above normal, with more rainfall than usual.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Safety expert urges new layer to lift system checks
articles.excerpt: An elevator-safety adviser has urged improvements to the city's three-tier inspection process after 720 lifts were found to be missing…
articles.fullText:
An elevator-safety adviser has urged improvements to the city's three-tier inspection process after 720 lifts were found to be missing fire-resistant door frame components.

Maxine Yao, a member of the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department’s lifts and escalators safety advisory committee, made the call after Taizoom Elevator was ordered to complete remedial works by the middle of November for two public housing estates and within two to three months for the private buildings.

The department's order followed the discovery that about 90 percent of lifts installed by Taizoom lacked the required door frame parts.

Speaking on an RTHK radio programme on Tuesday, Yao called the number of lifts involved shocking and said the current process for issuing use or resumption permits could be improved in light of the findings.

Under the existing three-tier system, a registered lift contractor carries out a self-inspection, a registered engineer performs an independent thorough examination and the department's engineers then conduct an on-site re-inspection and functional testing.

The city has long relied on an integrity-based system, Yao said, arguing that the mechanism could be strengthened with an additional step.

"This system has indeed been effective all along, except that in the whole industry this time two engineers of Taizoom had problems. If you ask whether we need to do better, I agree," she said.

"I have said I hope the department can introduce independent third-party inspection to add one more step in the middle tier to ensure public safety."

Yao also welcomed the department’s proposal to expand the digital video and photographic log-book system – currently used to record work details for lifts and escalators – to cover lift upgrades and replacements.

"The department has found that since we already have such a good system and platform, why not update it to include upgrading and replacing lifts too in response to public demand," she said.

"I think that is a very proactive plan."

Yao noted the system was still awaiting updates and said she hoped the department would complete the upgrade before the end of the year to prevent similar incidents from happening again.

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: China says trade surplus surpassed US$1tn in October
articles.excerpt: China's trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion for a second year in a row, according to official data released on Tuesday…
articles.fullText:
China's trade surplus exceeded US$1 trillion for a second year in a row, according to official data released on Tuesday.

The nation's foreign trade in goods maintained strong growth momentum in the first 10 months of 2026, with imports posting especially robust gains, according to official data.

Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year over the period, accelerating from 18.8 percent in the first nine months, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).

Exports jumped 35.2 percent year-on-year to US$412.3 billion last month, according to the GAC, while imports in October expanded 41.6 percent to US$307.1 billion.

Between January and October, the country logged a US$1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to US$105.3 billion from US$133.5 billion in September as imports picked up pace.

Analysts expect China to surpass the record US$1.2 trillion surplus it hit last year.

“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.

Meanwhile, exports to the United States surged 32.9 percent last month, the GAC data showed.

The figures come ahead of another meeting between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen next week.

The two have navigated a shaky truce to a trade war since their meeting in October 2025. They also met twice this year.

Beijing on Monday officially announced the extension of a trade truce with Washington due to expire on November 10 by two months, but said last week that expanding its purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of their agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.

"The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets," said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.

Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand.

Much of the strength in exports this year has been fuelled by a global push to expand AI infrastructure.

"The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last," Macquarie analysts wrote.

They expect China's exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before starting to slow from the first quarter of 2027. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: US military surrenders in court fight with WuXi AppTec
articles.excerpt: The US military has removed mainland biotechnology company WuXi AppTec from its list of Chinese military companies, according to a…
articles.fullText:
The US military has removed mainland biotechnology company WuXi AppTec from its list of Chinese military companies, according to a government posting.

The deputy secretary of defence made the determination on Monday in light of a federal court in Washington barring the department from enforcing the designation, the posting said.

The ruling came in a lawsuit WuXi AppTec filed after the Pentagon added it to the list, saying its designation was arbitrary, capricious, unsupported by the facts and "the product of political pressure".

The US military's headquarters at the Pentagon expanded its blacklist of alleged "Chinese military companies" on June 8 to 188 entities.

"This decision relieves the company from further adverse consequences of the 1260H designation," WuXi AppTec said in a filing to the Hong Kong bourse on Tuesday morning, referring to the list that is kept under section 1260H of a US defence law.

"We remain committed to serving our customers and enabling the lifesaving and life-improving medicines they make for patients," the company added. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: HK, regional markets get a bump from Wall St gains
articles.excerpt: Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he planned to…
articles.fullText:
Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he planned to hold off on new military strikes against Iran lifted sentiment ahead of US inflation data that could sway the near-term interest rate outlook.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened up 172 points, or 0.7 percent, at 24,621.

The China enterprises index rose 38 points, or 0.47 percent, to 8,298 while the tech index climbed 31 points, or 0.78 percent, to 4,072.

Two chip-sector firms debuted in Hong Kong, with AI chip designer Suzhou Denglin Technology falling into loss territory at the start of trading and semiconductor packager and tester Jiangsu Xinde Semiconductor Technology making a much stronger debut.

Across the border, the Shanghai Composite Index opened up 21 points, or 0.58 percent, at 3,682.

The Shenzhen Component Index put on 167 points, or 1.51 percent, to open at 11,313 while the ChiNext Index rose 59 points, or 2.44 percent, to 2,518.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 596 points, or 1.02 percent, higher at 59,372 and was 1,725 points or almost three percent higher at one stage before noon.

In Seoul, the Kospi surged 228 points, or 4.55 percent, to open at 5,247 amid gains for its heavyweight chipmakers – 3.74 percent for Samsung Electronics and 5.28 percent for SK Hynix.

The gains came as Brent crude futures were hovering at their lowest levels since early September, well below US$100 per barrel, as investors pinned their hopes on possible talks between the United States and Iran.

They were last down one percent at US$91.56 a barrel.

The US-Israeli war with Iran, which erupted at the end of February, has stoked inflationary concerns across the globe, spurring major central banks to raise rates in recent months.

Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global, said the latest developments offered hope that an end to the conflict could be approaching, but there was still a considerable gap between diplomacy and a lasting peace agreement.

"The risk now is that markets have moved too far, too quickly... any indication that negotiations are faltering could see a substantial rebound in prices as traders rapidly rebuild the geopolitical risk premium," he said.

The slump in oil prices eased inflation worries and helped lift stocks after last week's rout as a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

On Monday, the S&P 500 clocked its biggest one-day jump since April, closing up 2.35 percent while the Nasdaq closed 2.7 percent higher, its best day in over four months.

"We believe resets in expectations are healthy, and the AI trade appears to be working through a reset of its own at the moment," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise.

Earnings reports due this week from tech companies such as CoreWeave, a barometer of investor anxiety over AI, will be another test for markets as investors fret about the cost of the AI buildout.

Saglimbene said Anthropic's prospective IPO could be an important test of investor confidence.

Market focus remains on Nvidia after the second-most valuable company in the world said its board was probing whether CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation.

A media report alleged he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

Huang has said he was unfaithful to his wife.

Shares of Nvidia, which is due to report earnings next week, fell 4.2 percent.

Daniel Morgan, a portfolio manager at Synovus Trust who holds Nvidia shares, said certain personalities in the technology space were so intertwined with the success of the company it was hard to separate the two.

"But the companies can still be successful long after the original founders have taken on a lesser role," he said, adding he remained confident that Nvidia would continue to maintain its lead in the GPU AI chip market even if Huang was forced to step down to a lesser role.

All eyes will be on US inflation data later in the day, with prices likely to have increased at a moderate pace in October, economists said, and remaining stubbornly high enough for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates next month.

Traders are pricing in an 84 percent chance of a rate hike next month versus 74 percent a week earlier, a CME FedWatch tool showed after a blowout October jobs report on Friday. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: A trip to the South Korean seaside for glimpses of my North Korean hometown
articles.excerpt: Escapee Park Sol-ji often gets homesick for the port city of Chongjin. A beach day in Busan comes close.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Park Sol-ji stared out over the water at Gwangalli Beach with the iconic Gwangan Bridge in the distance, just above the horizon. South Korea’s touristy second largest city of Busan is a drastic change from heavily industrialized Chongjin – her hometown in North Korea. But both cities are large ports on the eastern side of the peninsula, and the sand, the breeze, and the smell of the sea reminds her of home.
“I love looking at the sea, and coming here whenever I miss my hometown is a big part of it,” she told Radio Free Asia Nov. 3. “Also, coming to the seaside makes me feel like I can finally breathe. I think I like it because it gives me such a sense of liberation.”
Park Sol-ji is a pseudonym she is using for safety reasons. Sol-ji fled North Korea 19 years ago when she was 20 years old, arriving in South Korea the following year. Adjusting to life in the fast-paced South was jarring. Though she tried her best to blend in among South Korean 20-somethings , it would all come crashing down whenever she spoke with her unmistakable North Korean accent.
She often found the degree of change in her life to be overwhelming, and she longed to return home, but that was now impossible. In times like that a trip to the sea would always remind her just enough of home to boost her spirits.
These days, she’s shed the accent and looks about the same as everyone else, but she still gets homesick and often travels to the seaside.
A map showing the locations of Chongjin, North Korea and Busan, South Korea.
(RFA) Busan is very different from Chongjin. Though both cities are industrialized ports, the South Korean city has – over many decades – invested in travel infrastructure and branded itself as a global tourist destination.
According to tourism statistics compiled by the Busan city government, more than 3.93 million foreign tourists have already visited Busan this year alone. CNN introduced Busan as “Asia’s Next Coastal City,” and Expedia selected Busan as the only Korean destination among its “Top 10 Destinations of the Year for 2027.”
But for Sol-ji, it’s not the glitz and glamor she’s coming for. She is here to take in the memories of the seaside of her childhood, where she played in the sand with her friends and spent precious moments with her family.
Memories roll in with the rising tide
Though the forecast called for cloudy weather, Gwangalli Beach had quite a few visitors from midday, perhaps due to the unexpectedly clear sky. Couples were taking photos with the sea as a backdrop, groups of noisy students on a field trip made their way across the sand, and foreign tourists walked barefoot. Everyone had smiles on their faces. Gwangalli Beach is well known as a romantic spot where the blue sea harmonizes with the spectacular night view of the Gwangan Bridge.
Sol-ji slowly surveyed the seascape and her face lit up as she spoke of the days she and her family would break out a large cauldron, build a fire, catch fish, and cook eojuk, a type of spicy fish porridge. She also remembered how she and her friends used to play by pulling up seaweed to gather in makeshift nets made of their extra clothes. Although these were ordinary childhood games, looking back now, they were moments she can never have again. To her, the sea is a landscape she longs for, as well as a place where she finds solace for her wounds.
“I even dreamt of returning to Chongjin because I missed my hometown, but even in the dream, seeing my dyed hair and decorated nails, I thought I would get caught,” she said. North Korea is notorious for fashion police who crack down on “capitalist” looks like dyed hair, colored nails, blue jeans, clothing with English words and phrases, and other no-nos. In South Korea, Sol-ji is free to dress how she wants to, but that does not erase her longing.
“I really do want to go back just once.”
The old village in the hills
Prior to visiting the beach, Sol-ji had started the day with a train ride to Busan Station, disembarking in the morning. The first spot on her itinerary was Gamcheon Culture Village, a 10-minute taxi ride away. The village started as a ramshackle town built up in the hills for laborers, and it expanded greatly with the swell of refugees fleeing to Busan from the advancing North Korean army in the opening weeks of the 1950-53 Korean War. In recent years the village was painstakingly restored through cultural preservation and beautification projects.
These days, tourists flock to its narrow meandering streets, attracted by the colorfully painted houses, many of which have been converted to shops, cafes and mini-museums. Near the high point of the village sits a colorful bronze statue of the Little Prince, presiding over a space dedicated to the mythos presented in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s world-renowned novella.
A statue of the Little Prince and the fox at the Little Prince House in Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea.
(Saha-gu Office via korea.net) Today, the tourists have come in force. More often than not, passersby who came for the village’s unique artsy flair will be speaking in a language other than Korean.
While most tourists are browsing the shops, ordering refreshments, or taking in one of the museums, Sol-ji slowly looks around the alley, finally focusing on a clothesline in the courtyard of one house. She noticed three or four items of clothing hanging on a single line, swaying in the breeze. It was this evidence that people actually live here that conjured up the feelings of her childhood.
“People here hang their laundry on clotheslines like that. It’s exactly the same in North Korea,” she said. She explained that in North Korea some families have washing machines, but rolling blackouts are common in most places, so people still have to do laundry by hand.
“So here they also dry their laundry in the sun,” she said. “Knowing this is quite heartwarming.”
In another area of town she operated a manual pump that once drew water out of the ground. She said it made her think of her grandmother’s house in Chongjin.
Sol-ji walked along, looking around every corner of the alley. Though sun-dried laundry and the hand pump might be similar details, the nature of this town, built up on a hillside, would never make sense in Chongjin, she said.
Park Sol-ji, visits Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “There aren’t many houses on slopes like this in Chongjin. It costs a lot of money to build roads and houses up to these inclines,” she said. “Instead, there are many fields on these mountain slopes. It is land where people make a living through farming.”
Noon approached, and it was time for lunch.
Food for reminiscing
Sol-ji’s next destination was the famous open-air Jagalchi seafood market. As she walked from stall to stall, the boisterous calls of merchants mingled together, as they tried to attract customers by shouting out prices in their folksy Busan accents while holding up wriggling fish. Jagalchi is the largest seafood market in the country, and it is another big Busan tourist destination.
Sol-ji looked around the market, carefully observing the fish leaping out of the ice. She seemed to be searching for familiar fish such as flounder, cutlassfish, mackerel, and squid. Although it was an unfamiliar market, the seafood displayed on the stalls was something she often saw back in her hometown, she said.
She recalled how North and South Koreans use different words for squid and two types of octopus and this led to confusion.
문어 (muneo) 낙지 (nakji) 오징어 (ojingeo)
North Korea all octopus varieties squid cuttlefish
South Korea large octopus varieties small octopus varieties squid and cuttlefish
“We called squid nakji . So when I’m here and I see the small octopus that they’re calling nakji , that’s what we used to call baby muneo ,” said Sol-ji.
She recalled that during her childhood she would often snack on dried squid, tearing off tasty parts and chewing it by the mouthful.
The marketplace also conjured up memories of eating raw fish, but the way she enjoyed it up North was very different. In Chongjin raw fish is served slathered in a thick sauce, and wrapped with other ingredients in lettuce. But she was surprised when she came to South Korea and saw people eat the plain white flesh dipped in only a little bit of sauce.
Park Sol-ji visits Jagalchi seafood market in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “I think the seafood I ate in Chongjin was tastier,” she said, smiling broadly. She explained that fish caught in colder places is saltier and tastier.
But then again, she said, it might have just been that she was hungry all the time back then.
“It’s like something out of a dream.”
As the sun set behind Gwangalli Beach, Gwangan Bridge lit up the night sky in a dazzling flash of color. Sol-ji got in line to ride a yacht under the bridge, out to sea to catch the fireworks show exclusively for the passengers.
Park Sol-ji views the city of Busan, South Korea at night off Gwangalli Beach, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) As the yacht moved along, Sol-ji couldn’t help but notice that it was a stark difference from the pitch black nighttime seascape in Chongjin – out at sea, Busan’s night sky is brightly and colorfully illuminated by the bridge, the cityscape – and soon, the fireworks.
Sol-ji sat on the deck, quietly closing her eyes and feeling the sea breeze. Then in one magic moment, lights shot out of the sky with a loud boom. The fireworks brought a bright smile across her face.
In all her excitement, her thoughts drifted to her childhood friends. Although they live in different places now, she thought how wonderful it would be if they could gaze at the dazzling night sea of ​​Busan together.
A yacht tour fireworks display in the waters off Gwangalli Beach in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
(RFA) “This really feels like a dream, but I really do want to try it with them at least once,” she said. “I want to take lots of photos with my friends and go sightseeing like this.”
Under the glowing bursts, she reflected on her current daily life. Nothing like this would ever be possible in North Korea, she said. But in South Korea she can go wherever she wants, with whomever she wants, wearing whatever she wants. She smiled, realizing that “freedom” isn’t a grandiose ideal or political buzzword, it is contained in an ordinary moment like this, on a boat at sea near Busan, under the brightly lit night sky.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Harris Ho wins HK's second gold at Youth Olympics
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong, China fencer Harris Ho on Tuesday bagged the city's second gold medal of the Youth Olympics Games in…
articles.fullText:
Hong Kong, China fencer Harris Ho on Tuesday bagged the city's second gold medal of the Youth Olympics Games in Senegal, winning the individual men's foil final in dominant fashion.

Ho, the reigning world junior foil champion, defeated Japan's Masashi Maeda 15-8 in the gold medal bout at the Dakar Expo Centre.

The 17-year-old's triumph marks the SAR's first-ever individual fencing gold in the history of the Youth Olympics, with the city having previously claimed two fencing silvers in the 2014 and 2018 editions of the quadrennial event.

Ho's win caps off a dominant run in the competition, going five and one in the group stage to enter the quarter-finals as the second seed.

The SAR star brushed aside the Czech Republic's Krystof Novak 15-2 in the quarter-finals, before beating Cyprus's Aris Kiayias 15-10 in the last four.

The landmark victory also builds on a phenomenal year for Ho, who won the Cadet World Championship title in April, and further cements him as a top contender ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law congratulated him on capturing gold in Senegal.

"With an outstanding performance at the Youth Olympic Games this year, he overcame his opponents to secure the gold medal and set a historic milestone for a young Hong Kong fencing athlete. All of the Hong Kong citizens take great pride in his remarkable achievement," she said in a statement.
