articles.title: Trump says Qatar, Saudi prefer peace in Iran conflict
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump said on Monday he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister in White House talks.

Trump, in a Reuters interview and a later appearance in the White House press briefing room, said he plans to keep up a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz for now.

"The United States of America is fully locked and loaded with the best equipment ever made, and we don't think there's going to be any reason to use it," Trump told reporters.

He said he was acting "at the behest of countries that are their neighbours" and specifically cited Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and others that prefer the US not to launch new attacks.

Trump spoke after meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, a key intermediary with Tehran, as efforts to end the war ramp up following last week's US midterm elections.

More than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on February 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan. Senior US and Gulf officials have cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.

Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.

Al-Thani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of Qatar, met Trump after visiting Tehran last week.

The prime minister called his talks with both Trump and Vice President JD Vance positive.

"Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region," he said on X.

Iranian security council chief Mohsen Rezaei said on X the US should "stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks" and that it was "time to surrender to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out."

Iran's proposal to end the war involves an end to the US blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme and other sanctions to follow.

The US has repeatedly rejected that plan, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing Tehran's conditions on Sunday as "outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic."

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei defended the plan on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table.

Senior US Republicans including Vance have blamed their party's losses in last week's elections on the Iran war. Despite the growing domestic political pressure to end the conflict, Rubio said he did not believe a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.

A senior United Arab Emirates official, Anwar Gargash, echoed that view on Monday, saying a comprehensive political settlement between the US and Iran appeared difficult.

"We should... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted," he said.

Vance, who led the negotiations for a short-lived truce in June, will also meet Al-Thani, whose country has been a prime mediator since early in the war, conveying messages between the sides and proposing ways to bridge their differences.

Anxiety over the war has pervaded the region for months, and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday he had told Trump that Ankara did not want to see a new escalation.

"We emphasise at every opportunity that it is possible to resolve these issues through dialogue and diplomacy. Unfortunately, we see a negative shift once again. We are doing our utmost to prevent this," Erdogan told reporters. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Krakow holds silent march after mass shooting
articles.excerpt: Thousands of people took part in a silent march through Krakow on Monday evening along with Poland's president and prime…
articles.fullText:
Thousands of people took part in a silent march through Krakow on Monday evening along with Poland's president and prime minister as the country tries to come to terms with an unprecedented mass shooting, in which a Polish man killed six people on the southern city's main square.

Relations between Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki are tense, but they appear to want a display of national unity over an incident that has shocked Poland and left rival political camps bitterly disputing the killer's motives.

"For Poland, this is always a sign of hope: that while we may hold different views, we are still capable of cooperating, engaging in dialogue, and seeking out what unites us," Deputy Prime Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told TVN24.

"We are capable of showing solidarity during difficult times. Together, we can support those who need such support," he added.

March participants followed part of the route the shooter drove while firing and lit memorial candles at the spots where people were killed on Saturday.

"Tonight in Cracow thousands of Poles gathered to pay tribute to the victims of November 7 attack," Tusk wrote on X.

The suspected gunman died in hospital on Monday after being shot and arrested by police minutes after they said he opened fire from his car in Krakow's historic main square, a popular tourist destination.

The government said the man, identified by prosecutors as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski from the southeastern town of Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, may have been inspired by far-right ideology. But officials appeared to backtrack on Monday.

"Until the matter is fully clarified and the authorities are in possession of complete information, it is best to refrain from making comments, even if there are some initial indications," government spokesperson Adam Szlapka told TVN24.

Both the shooter and his father held gun permits, and several firearms were found in the family apartment and the assailant's car, prosecutors said.

The bodies of his father, mother and sister were found in their family home on Saturday, and officials say they were also likely killed by Oksinski.

The nationalist opposition rejected the suggestion of a far-right link to the killings, with Law and Justice party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski saying those claims were a "blatant lie."

National Prosecutor's Office spokesperson Przemyslaw Nowak told a press conference that investigators did not yet know what motivated the killer.

He said that a yellow flag featuring a snake and the words "Don't tread on me," known as the Gadsden flag, was found in Oksinski's room.

The Gadsden flag was first used during the American Revolution in the 18th century. Nowak said the flag was associated with "various meanings related to freedom or rebellion" but was not widely known as being linked to any form of extremism.

Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said there were many different emblems on the perpetrator's clothing that had already been partially examined and interpreted.

Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said despite the death of the shooter, the investigation would continue, and would aim to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group.

"Evidence is being collected, but I will not show or disclose it. I ask for restraint," Zurek told Radio Zet.

Poland's Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime (CBZC) said it had detained five Polish citizens and one Ukrainian who had posted threatening or alarming content online following the attack. It said the detainees were aged 15 to 36.

Galecka said the CBZC and the police were on high alert for potential copycats.

Poland had never experienced such a mass shooting. Scenes of blood and bodies strewn across the historic heart of one of its main tourist attractions have shocked a nation that has long viewed itself as safer than Western European neighbours that have experienced similar attacks.

"A total of four firearms and several hundred rounds of ammunition were discovered in the vehicle and in the possession of Michal Oksinski," Nowak said.

"We secured a very large number of spent casings. In total, at least several dozen shots were fired – possibly even several hundred."

Nowak said the two police officers injured in the attack had regained consciousness.

Tusk wrote on X that when police officer Artur Moranski woke up, his first words were, "Is Kuba alive?" – referring to fellow injured officer Jakub Kulik.

The government will review regulations on requirements for people with gun permits following the tragedy, Zurek said. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: France says Iran behind fridge cyberattacks
articles.excerpt: France on Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind cyberattacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing…
articles.fullText:
France on Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind cyberattacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing sanctions on a European level against Tehran over the first such large-scale cyber sabotage on French territory.

Numerous French supermarkets were hit in the October 11 and 12 cyberattacks, which raised the temperatures in their refrigerators, in some cases forcing them to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.

"I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said of the cyberattacks.

"This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," he said on the sidelines of the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris.

The Paris prosecutor said in a separate statement she had opened an investigation into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit of the IRGC, over the attacks.

The cyber monitoring centre of four French security agencies said the unit is better known in the cyber world as CyberAveng3rs, its avatar through which it has claimed attacks in the past.

"It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people," said Barrot.

"We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible," he added.

Barrot directly referred only to attacks against French supermarket systems, which he said targeted 700 sites.

However, similar incidents have been reported in other European countries.

On November 2, grocery stores across at least nine other European countries were hit by a suspected cyberattack on their freezer systems.

The incidents have shaken Europe at a time when officials have warned of the risk of cyberattacks from Russia while European countries press for support of Ukraine in its war against Moscow.

In recent days, European air traffic has also been disrupted by false bomb alerts against dozens of flights, although the origin of those threats has yet to be made clear.

The United States and Israel fought a war against Iran that began with the killing of supreme leader Ali Khamenei on February 28.

European countries did not get involved in that conflict, but French officials have accused Iran of spreading misinformation related to the protests that have rocked France over the past month.

"It does not surprise us," responded US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who is attending the talks in Paris. "They (Iran) have done things like this for a very long time."

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement that a judicial investigation had been opened against the head of Shahid Kaveh and his two deputies.

She described the entity as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Centre of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-CEC)".

France's Centre for Coordination of Cyber Crises, which groups together security agencies including the intelligence services, said the unit "conducts large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for the purpose of sabotage, directed primarily against Israel and the United States, but also against France and other European countries".

It named the men involved as Hamid Reza Lashgarian, who heads the IRGC-CEC cyberattacks branch of the IRGC and Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, who lead the Shahid Kaveh operation.

The US Treasury in 2024 announced sanctions against Hamid Reza Lashgarian and Mahdi Lashgarian as well as four other individuals over cyberattacks. It described Hamid Reza Lashgarian as a commander in the IRGC's Quds force, which handles its foreign operations.

"A hallmark of this unit's modus operandi is the use of the Persian language and IP addresses that trace back to terminals located in Iran," said the Paris prosecutor.

She said attackers had taken control of the equipment remotely via web interfaces "to initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles".

Meanwhile, security alerts from sensors designed to go off when temperatures exceeded a certain threshold were "simultaneously disabled", she added.

Barrot said France had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris "to lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".

"We will take any other necessary and proportionate measures – whether public or otherwise – to respond to this incident and deter anyone who might seek to repeat it," he added.

Speaking after Barrot, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that "our response should be strong". (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: 22 migrants die trying to reach Greek island of Crete
articles.excerpt: At least 22 people died in two days in migrant boats trying to reach the Greek island of Crete, authorities…
articles.fullText:
At least 22 people died in two days in migrant boats trying to reach the Greek island of Crete, authorities said on Monday, warning of a migrant "crisis" on the island.

Twelve bodies were found on Monday on one boat off Crete's southern coast – a magnet for arrivals from Libya, the coastguard said. Another body was found in the sea and one of 18 people rescued from the boat died in hospital, a coastguard spokesman said.

The agency said the boat appeared to have been at sea for several days and autopsies would determine the cause of the deaths.

With high winds whipping up waves, eight bodies were found on another boat in the same zone 10 nautical miles off southern Crete on Sunday, the coast guard said.

Twenty-eight Sudanese nationals were taken off the boat, according to port authorities.

Survivors told investigators they had left Libya on November 3 or 4.

Two of the Sudanese, one aged 16, have been arrested on suspicion of people smuggling, authorities said.

In total, 105 people were rescued from three different boats on Monday by the Greek coastguard and the European Union's Frontex border agency, port authorities said.

Last week, a major operation was launched to find 59 people declared missing by a survivor after a boat capsized off Crete. No bodies have been found.

Crete has become a key entry point for migrants trying to reach Europe by making the dangerous crossing from Libya.

The UN's International Organization for Migration has said the growing number of attempted crossings has exposed gaps in search and rescue capabilities.

Greece's Migration Minister Thanos Plevris, a right-wing hardliner on immigration, said on Friday that the country was preparing for "a crisis in Crete."

He said there had been 1,700 arrivals in the first three days of November alone and condemned the "total lack of cooperation" by Libyan authorities to stop the migrant boats.

In response to that influx, the government has announced plans to open a temporary housing complex near Heraklion, the island's largest city.

According to the United Nations refugee agency, more than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece in 2026 so far. More than 22,000 of those people landed on Crete, the country's largest island. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: S Arabia says crucial pipeline hit but still working
articles.excerpt: Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, essential for bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, was attacked on Monday but operations were unaffected…
articles.fullText:
Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, essential for bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, was attacked on Monday but operations were unaffected, official media said, as the kingdom and Yemen's Houthis trade strikes.

The Saudi Press Agency cited an official with the energy ministry as saying the pipeline was targeted in the Medina region in the west of the country, causing a "limited fire" that was extinguished.

"No injuries or fatalities were reported, and pipeline operations were unaffected," the report said.

The report did not say who was responsible, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles.

The East-West pipeline, which enables the world's largest crude exporter to get its oil to market via the Red Sea, has taken on increased significance since the outbreak of the Middle East war as Iran seeks to choke off the main route for Gulf energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Earlier on Monday, Saudi authorities warned Riyadh residents of "a hostile aerial threat," a day after an attack on a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco rattled the capital's business district.

"Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors, and follow the instructions of the Civil Defence," the alert said, before the warning was lifted minutes later.

Saudi Arabia has faced near-daily strikes from the Houthis for weeks after a truce in their long-running conflict unravelled in July.

On Monday evening, parents of students were alerted that schools in Riyadh were returning to online classes "as part of the ongoing precautionary measures".

Students had only been back in the classroom for two days following weeks of distance learning, and the message to parents did not say how long the new interval was expected to last.

The Houthis, who control large parts of Yemen, Saudi Arabia's impoverished southern neighbour, did not announce a fresh attack on Riyadh on Monday.

But they did report a Saudi strike on Hodeida airport on the Red Sea, which has long been out of use.

The Houthis' Almasirah television said the death toll from weekend Saudi strikes on a village in Sanaa province had climbed to 44, including more than 20 children.

On Sunday, the Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh's business district, where witnesses said Aramco Tower was damaged.

Saudi authorities said the building suffered minor damage from falling shrapnel after an "attempted attack."

The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Aramco tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company's headquarters.

A Saudi-led coalition initially launched hostilities with the Houthis in March 2015, months after the group seized the capital Sanaa, forcing out Yemen's internationally recognised government. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Millions fill Buenos Aires streets to greet Pope Leo
articles.excerpt: Vast crowds thronged one of the main boulevards in Buenos Aires on Monday as Pope Leo hailed the strength of…
articles.fullText:
Vast crowds thronged one of the main boulevards in Buenos Aires on Monday as Pope Leo hailed the strength of the Catholic Church in South America at an outdoor Mass that drew a record 2.5 million people on the first papal trip to Argentina in 39 years.

Argentines stretched for miles down Avenida del Libertador, waving the white-and-yellow Vatican flag and pressing against security barriers for a glimpse of the pontiff. It was the largest event to date of the pope's 18-month tenure leading the global Catholic Church.

Chants of "Long live Pope Leo!" echoed down the tree-lined street as the pope, on the second leg of a 12-day trip to South America, was driven by in an open-top popemobile under sunny skies.

Leo said in his sermon how happy he was to see Catholics in a region that has long been a stronghold for the Church but where it has been losing ground recently to fast-growing evangelical denominations.

"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," said the pope. "My visit to this land of Argentina has allowed me to see on your faces the enthusiasm of your faith."

Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 50-event, three-country tour less than a month after undergoing lung cancer surgery. He visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday and will travel on to Peru on Wednesday before returning to Rome on November 17.

The first US-born pope spent decades as a missionary in Peru and the Vatican has described the tour, one of the most demanding foreign tours by a pope in decades, as a "homecoming".

People had gathered in the early hours of Monday ahead of the Mass. Some normally bustling parts of the city stood near-empty as police cordoned off a security zone.

"I love that (Leo) is visiting us," said Claudia Pardo, 37, who waited for Leo with her husband and two young children. "It's a unique, historic moment, and we should listen to his message."

Alejandra Frias, 56, was sleepless after camping out all night to get a front-row view of the pope. "This is an emotional and spiritual moment," she said.

A pope has not visited majority-Catholic Argentina since 1987. Francis, Leo's predecessor, never made it back to his home country after ascending to the papacy.

Leo has emerged as a forceful voice on the world stage, lamenting what he sees as a failure of global leadership. On his tour he has urged South American nations to set an example of regional cooperation and patient diplomacy instead of conflict.

On Sunday, the pope addressed Argentine President Javier Milei, a libertarian and ally of US President Donald Trump. He urged Milei, who has pushed an austerity agenda that the Church has strongly criticised for cutting social services, to not target Argentina's poorest.

He also told Milei, a theatrical figure known for bombastic statements, that leaders should be careful with their words and know the limits of their power.

The pope lamented the difficulties faced by Argentine families at the Mass on Monday. He said they are enduring "instability, social hardship, precarious employment, domestic violence, painful separations and addictions that destroy young people's futures and damage family relationships."

Later, in a meeting with labourers and union leaders, the pope decried corporate greed and urged that workers be treated with respect. "The economy... must be at the service of the person, and not the person at the service of the economy," he said to applause from the group.

The pope, who has warned that artificial intelligence could lead the world down a path of unending war, also expressed concern that "unregulated automation can put countless jobs at risk."

Leo also met on Monday with five victims of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy, one of several such meetings he is expected to have on his trip as the Church seeks to repair its standing after abuse scandals tarnished its reputation. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Nvidia plunges as tech shares rebound, oil slides
articles.excerpt: US stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 rebound…
articles.fullText:
US stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 rebound from its biggest weekly drop since April 2025, and tech shares jumped even as AI heavyweight Nvidia slumped with controversy swirling around CEO Jensen Huang.

Last week, stocks slumped after a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

Markets were in rally mode even as Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, tumbled over 4 percent and closed at its lowest level since April 7. Investors questioned CEO Huang's future at the AI chipmaker after an internal investigation was launched into whether a foreign intelligence effort had targeted him.

China has dismissed the spying allegation as a baseless smear.

"The AI story is not going away if people are worried about that, the Democrats are not going to destroy AI. They can't. It's got a life of its own. They can put regulation around it, but they're certainly not stopping it," said Ken Polcari, partner and chief market strategist at SlateStone Wealth in Jupiter, Florida.

Providing further support was a sharp drop in crude oil prices that helped dampen concerns about price pressures, as US President Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran.

"Oil prices for sure, if they're down, that's certainly adding fuel to the fire," said Polcari.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,104 points, or 2.2 percent, to 52,389, the S&P 500 gained 173 points, or 2.4 percent, to 7,549 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 673 points, or 2.7 percent, to 25,253.

The S&P recorded its biggest daily percentage gain since April 8, while the Nasdaq marked its biggest daily advance since July 30.

Inflation readings are on the docket this week as the US Labour Department will release its Consumer Price Index report for October on Tuesday and Producer Price Index on Friday.

Some analysts on Wall Street also viewed last week's decline as an overreaction. Morgan Stanley and UBS said last week's rout in AI stocks was overdone, and risks were low of extreme regulation of data centre developments, even with Democratic majorities in the US Congress.

Even as oil prices have eased, expectations for a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December policy meeting remain above 80 percent, according to CME FedWatch, as October's strong jobs report gave the central bank latitude to continue raising rates.

Chipmakers surged. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index shot up 6.9 percent after plunging more than 12 percent last week, its biggest weekly drop since the week ended April 4, 2025. Nvidia was the sole decliner in the index on Monday, while Broadcom, up 8.8 percent, and Advanced Micro Devices, up 13.3 percent, were the two biggest boosts.

Shares of investment giant KKR advanced 1.7 percent after its quarterly profit hit a record high. Constellation Energy, an energy firm with exposure to the AI buildout, shot up more than 10 percent after its adjusted third-quarter profit surpassed expectations. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Republican launches impeachment against Pete Hegseth
articles.excerpt: A Republican lawmaker moved on Monday to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up…
articles.fullText:
A Republican lawmaker moved on Monday to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress just days after US President Donald Trump's party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.

Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.

The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as Wednesday, with some lawmakers from Trump's party signalling that they might join Democrats in supporting the charges.

Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for Hegseth and the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove him from office.

That would require a trial and conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate – a far higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

The impeachment push has gathered momentum since last Tuesday's midterm elections, when Democrats swept both chambers of Congress amid widespread anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.

Republicans retain control of Congress until the newly elected lawmakers take office on January 3, but their overwhelming defeat has fuelled recriminations and weakened party discipline.

Some Republican lawmakers who lost their seats could also skip votes, potentially making it easier for the impeachment measure to pass.

Massie, an outspoken critic of Trump who lost his own primary to a candidate backed by the president, is using a special congressional procedure to force the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.

Republican leaders could still seek to block the measure through a procedural vote.

The articles accuse Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which limits the president's ability to engage US forces in hostilities without congressional approval.

They also allege misconduct involving civilian casualties and military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.

The Pentagon has rejected the accusations.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker in January, threw his weight behind impeachment on Sunday.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC News.

"The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," he said.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Several Republicans have expressed dissatisfaction with Hegseth's leadership without committing to impeaching him.

Arkansas congressman French Hill said on Sunday he wanted to hear the debate before deciding whether the accusations justified impeachment.

Under the US Constitution, the House can impeach a senior government official by a simple majority vote, effectively bringing formal charges of serious misconduct.

The Senate then decides whether to convict and remove the official from office, requiring support from two-thirds of senators present.

Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold. Only two Cabinet secretaries – almost 150 years apart – have been impeached in US history, and neither was removed by the Senate.

Hegseth has dismissed Massie's impeachment effort as a "sham," calling the congressman "disgruntled" and accusing his opponents of pursuing political destruction.

The Pentagon announced a rare press briefing by Hegseth scheduled for Tuesday.

Trump has publicly stood by his embattled defence chief, declaring last week: "I have every intention to keep him."

But the president's weakened political position after the midterms has left Hegseth facing the prospect of an impeachment battle that could extend well beyond this week's House vote. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: Russell Brand jailed for 10 years for rape, assault
articles.excerpt: British comedian and TV star Russell Brand was on Monday jailed for more than 10 years for a string of…
articles.fullText:
British comedian and TV star Russell Brand was on Monday jailed for more than 10 years for a string of sex offences including rape as the judge told him he had been a "sexual predator" whose fame had protected him.

Brand, 51, showed no emotion as judge Joel Bennathan said he had acted with "staggering arrogance" and shown "contempt" for his victims who had suffered significant and lasting harm.

Paying tribute to the "bravery" of the women who came forward, the judge told Brand he had acted "how you liked and when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live."

His wife Laura Gallacher, with whom he has three children, slumped in her seat in the public gallery of London's Southwark Crown Court as the total sentence of 10 years and six months was announced.

Brand told his wife, who has supported him in court throughout the case, "we'll be OK" as he was led down to the cells.

The disgraced star was convicted by a jury last week of one rape and three sexual assaults committed against four women between 2004 and 2009.

The sentence marks the final fall in a scandal-hit showbiz career that saw him embody the anything-goes culture of 2000s British TV and radio.

Brand, who has reinvented himself as an online Christian guru, held a string of prayer beads and made the sign of the cross before one of his victims personally read out her impact statement from behind a screen.

The woman said she had been left "traumatised" by the assault in a London bar in 2004.

"For many years as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behaviour against women like it was all a joke," she told the court. Brand listened impassively, looking straight ahead.

A second woman, a 21-year-old fan he raped in 2009 after they met at one of his shows, told the court she had felt she simply would "not be believed" if she reported him.

"His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless," she said, adding the consequences of the rape had "affected almost every aspect of my life."

The hearing came as Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the victims' bravery would bring about wider changes to the legal system.

Burnham pledged to be "relentless in making whatever improvements we can" to provide more support for victims, including setting up teams in every police force for handling rapes and serious sexual offences.

Brand was cleared of two other alleged rapes and one count of attempted indecent assault. But he is facing further investigations after London police said it was probing rape allegations by two more women.

From Channel 4 to MTV and an eponymous primetime show on BBC Radio 2, the wild-haired comedian worked for major British media houses in the 2000s, where his obsession with sex contributed to his notoriety.

Brand denied the charges, but he admitted to being "extremely promiscuous" and using his fame to "facilitate sexual access."

Born to working-class parents in Essex, east of London in 1975, Brand dropped out of drama school before joining MTV at the age of 25.

He had his own radio show at the BBC, which last week apologised for the "culture and failings" when Brand worked there between 2006 and 2008.

Brand left the BBC after sending a well-known actor sexually explicit messages about having slept with his granddaughter.

He made a foray into Hollywood after a brief marriage in 2010 to US pop star Katy Perry, followed by a stint as a left-wing commentator and campaigner.

The court found him guilty of sexual assaults against an MTV worker, a Channel 4 worker and a Capital Radio employee, as well as raping a fan.

The organisations that propped up Brand for years are now facing questions about how he continued for so long.

British culture minister Lisa Nandy on Sunday said men in power were still exploiting women in the media industry, saying his case was a "wake-up call." (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox…
articles.fullText:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here .

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. 

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
articles.excerpt: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning…
articles.fullText:
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

articles.title: Harris Ho wins 2nd gold for HK, China
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Culture, Sports & Tourism Rosanna Law today congratulated fencer Harris Ho on winning a gold medal in the…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Culture, Sports & Tourism Rosanna Law today congratulated fencer Harris Ho on winning a gold medal in the Men's Foil Individual at the 4th Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal.

The victory marks the first gold medal ever won by the Hong Kong, China fencing team at the Games and the second gold medal won by the Hong Kong, China Delegation this year.

Miss Law noted that the triumph adds to Mr Ho's recent string of major successes. Earlier this year, he won a gold medal in the Cadet Boys' Foil Individual (U17) at the 2026 World Junior & Cadet Fencing Championships in April and a silver medal as part of the Men's Foil Team at the Asian Games in September.

“With an outstanding performance at the Youth Olympic Games this year, he overcame his opponents to secure the gold medal and set a historic milestone for a young Hong Kong fencing athlete.

“All Hong Kong citizens take great pride in his remarkable achievement,” Miss Law added.

​The 4th Youth Olympic Games are taking place from October 31 to November 13. Hong Kong sent a total of 15 athletes to compete in 12 sports and has so far won two gold, one silver and three bronze medals.

articles.title: Disney, Adobe strike deal to co-develop AI models
articles.excerpt: Disney and Adobe have struck a multi-year deal to co-develop custom generative AI models for the media giant with the…
articles.fullText:
Disney and Adobe have struck a multi-year deal to co-develop custom generative AI models for the media giant with the goal of scaling AI tools across its theme parks, studio and sports media businesses.

The move, announced on Monday, will start with speeding up project development timelines at Disney's Experiences division, home to its global theme parks, resorts and cruise lines, and for concept exploration at StudioLAB, the innovation hub within Walt Disney Studios.

Adobe will also work with Disney to use AI tools to boost engagement with sports fans at ESPN and bring more of ESPN's content archive to audiences.

Through Adobe's Firefly Foundry, which lets enterprises build and deploy custom AI models, the two companies will work on gen-AI models trained on Disney's intellectual properties that will generate production-ready outputs. The models will be private and proprietary to Disney.

Walt Disney Imagineering, the creative, design, and research and development arm behind Disney Experiences, has deployed a custom image generation model and a sketch-to-image model that can turn hand-drawn sketches into fully-rendered concept art.

"We talk about the time frames in our projects in years – it's years' worth of development. And what Adobe Foundry has allowed us to do is compress the creative process that would have taken months to now being able to do that in hours and days," Kyle Laughlin, senior vice president of R&D technology and engineering at Disney, said in an interview.

"We're able to run through multiple iterations quickly with these tools. And that helps us reduce costly changes in the field once we get into the construction of these experiences," Laughlin said, adding that the tools will help accelerate creative development at Disney and are "in no way meant to replace" roles at Imagineering.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg News reported that Disney was considering cutting thousands of jobs and has asked some managers to target 20 percent in annual cost savings. (Reuters)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Contractors get non-compliance notice over MTR project
articles.excerpt: The MTR Corporation said on Monday that it had issued a non-compliance notice to the contractors in charge of the…
articles.fullText:
The MTR Corporation said on Monday that it had issued a non-compliance notice to the contractors in charge of the Tung Chung West station construction.

This came after around 30 columns there were found to be substandard.

The railway operator said that it is strictly following up on the mistakes by the relevant contractors, the way they handled the matter and issues over responsibilities.

The company is now awaiting a comprehensive report from contractors, along with a remedial proposal.

The MTR said it attaches great importance towards railway projects’ supervision and work quality, and it will continue to carry out inspections as well as adopt other monitoring measures to ensure quality.

The firm will continue to maintain close contact with relevant government departments to ensure that the safety and quality of the works meet the contractual standards during construction and upon completion.

It added that it will fully cooperate with the government to probe the incident, and submit a report on time on the cause, remedial plan, as well as the follow-up actions with contractors.

The MTR reiterated that it will not tolerate any substandard engineering practices, and it will seriously follow up on the matter.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made 

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising.  Read the full story .

Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests  

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.

The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree.

For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.

Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate.

—Matthew Ponsford

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss
Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. ( NYT $)
+ Shares in Nvidia were down 5% in pre-market trading. ( CNBC )
+ Huang’s children are also employed by Nvidia. ( WSJ $)

2 Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech

articles.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
articles.excerpt: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new…
articles.fullText:
As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”

Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

More than 3,000 participants are expected to join an annual forum held by the Trade Development Council to exchange ideas on intellectual property (IP) development and hunt for business opportunities.

The Business of IP Asia Forum will be staged at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai on November 19 and 20.

Themed “Powering Commercial Success Through IP and Innovation”, the council’s associate executive director Silas Chu said nearly 100 speakers will discuss how IP and innovation can be used to build competitive advantages and draw capital investments, among others.

He said that for the first time, the forum will include a new chapter centred on IP commercialisation that aims to better help enterprises manage their IP.

“Previously in the BIP Asia forum, we may be focusing more on creative IP,” Chu said.

“But as Hong Kong moves towards the goal of becoming an international I&T centre, we are increasingly seeing a lot of interesting development, especially in the area of AI, in the area of life science and all those deep tech. There will be surging demand as a result.”

A startup from the Education University, which is pioneering their AI-enabled storytelling robot to help with students’ learning, is joining the forum.

Its director Hades Ho said he hopes to talk to potential clients and experts on how to expand the use of their project.

“Now our robot is mainly focused on the education aspect. But to be honest, this robot can [be] used in other aspects, for example, we have some further research on elderly, how to use this robot on elderly,” he said.

The Entrepreneur Day that features more than 370 startups and innovation projects across 14 countries and regions will be held alongside the two-day forum, allowing companies that have just kick-started their operations to conduct business matching and to help them expand.

articles.title: 41 stranded in mid-air as Ocean Park Tower ride stalls
articles.excerpt: Dozens of visitors had to be rescued from Ocean Park's observation tower ride on Monday afternoon, after the cabin malfunctioned…
articles.fullText:
Dozens of visitors had to be rescued from Ocean Park's observation tower ride on Monday afternoon, after the cabin malfunctioned and stopped mid-air.

The theme park said the 72-metre-tall sightseeing tower stopped working at about 2pm after a safety mechanism was triggered following a signal failure. The Fire Services Department said it had been alerted to the incident at around 3.30pm.

Ocean Park staff used about two hours to evacuate 40 trapped people via a safety passage located at the centre of the tower.

Meanwhile, one person with impaired mobility and who reported feeling unwell was taken to the ground by firefighters in about three minutes.

The director of Electrical and Mechanical Services, Poon Kwok-ying, said the department would investigate the incident to determine the cause, while the park said it will carry out a comprehensive inspection and tests to ensure safety.

This is the second incident involving the ride in about a year and a half, with the tower attraction also brought to a halt in May 2025, when its safety mechanism was triggered.

Passengers were stranded for nearly two hours then.

The tower, located about 200 metres above sea level, sits on Nam Long Shan and offers panoramic views of Deep Water Bay.
